children.text: Spinal tuberculosis, also known as Pott's disease, is a spinal infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can lead to osteomyelitis, kyphotic deformity, and mechanical instability
Diagnosis is made with a CT-guided biopsy evaluated for acid-fast bacilli

Treatment is usually bracing and anti-tuberculosis antibiotics in the absence of neurological defects or mechanical instability. Surgical management is indicated in the presence of neurological deficits, progressive kyphosis, and/or mechanical instability
increasing incidence in the U.S. due to a growing immunocompromised population
HIV-positive (often seen in patients with CD4+ counts of 50-200)
15% of patients with TB will have extrapulmonary involvement
the spine, and specifically the thoracic spine, is the most common extrapulmonary site
5% of all TB patients have spine involvement
begins in the metaphysis of the vertebral body
spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament, leading to
usually anterior and can be large (much more common in TB than in pyogenic infections)
initially does not involve the disc space (distinguishing it from pyogenic osteomyelitis, but can be misdiagnosed as a neoplastic lesion)
mean deformity in nonoperative cases is 15°
higher rate of kyphosis progression when the vertebral body and posterior elements are involved
granulomatous spinal infections are often diagnosed late and with more severe kyphosis compared to pyogenic infections
kyphosis progresses in 40% of cases because of growth spurts
type I: increase in deformity until cessation of growth
type II: decreasing progression with growth
type III: minimal change during either active or healed phases
onset of symptoms is typically more insidious than that of pyogenic infections
often a late symptom that only occurs after significant bony destruction and deformity
neurologic deficits (present in 10-47% of patients with Pott's disease)
mechanical pressure on the cord by abscess, granulation tissue, tubercular debris, or caseous tissue
mechanical instability from subluxation or dislocation
paraplegia from healed disease can occur with severe deformity
stenosis from ossification of the ligamentum flavum adjacent to severe kyphosis
indicated for any patient in whom TB is a possibility
involvement of the anterior vertebral body with **sparing of the disc space** (this can differentiate TB from a pyogenic infection)
lucency and compression of adjacent vertebral bodies, disc space destruction, and development of severe kyphosis
risk factors for buckling collapse ("spine-at-risk signs")
preferred imaging study for diagnosis and treatment planning
low signal on T1-weighted images, bright signal on T2-weighted images
presence of a septated prevertebral, paravertebral, and/or intraosseous, smooth-walled abscess with a subligamentous extension and breaching of the epidural space
high signal intensity of the disc on the T2-weighted image
demonstrates lesions <1.5 cm better than radiographs
obtain with a combination of technetium and gallium
shown to have the highest sensitivity for detecting infection
usually elevated, but may be normal in up to 25%
CT-guided biopsy with cultures and staining is effective at obtaining a diagnosis
mycobacteria (acid-fast bacilli) may take 10 weeks to grow in culture
PCR allows for faster identification (95% sensitivity and 93% accuracy)
Other etiologies of granulomatous infection may have a clinical picture similar to TB
medical therapy is the mainstay of treatment in most cases
isoniazid (H), rifampin (R), ethambutol (E), and pyrazinamide (Z) therapy
RHZE for 2 months, then RH for 9-18 months
may be used for pain control and prevention of deformity
anterior decompression/corpectomy, strut grafting ± posterior instrumented stabilization ± posterior column shortening
≥3 vertebrae involved with loss of ≥1.5 vertebral bodies in the thoracic spine
children ≤7 y/o with ≥3 affected vertebral bodies in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine and ≥2 at risk signs are likely to have progression and should undergo correction
cosmetic correction of kyphosis is controversial
advanced disease with **caseation** preventing antibiotic access
failure of nonoperative treatment after 3-6 months
in patients with neurologic deficits, early debridement and decompression can lead to improved neurologic recovery
autogenous and allograft strut grafts are acceptable with good results
continued medical management with isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide
chronic implant colonization is less common in TB and other granulomatous infections than in pyogenic infections

abscess/bony sequestra have a better prognosis than meningomyelitis
